item.title: Pakistan President Zardari congratulates Fakhrul, invites him to Pakistan
item.description:
Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari has congratulated Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on his election as Bangladesh President and invited him to visit Pakistan to further strengthen bilateral relations.

In a congratulatory message, Zardari expressed confidence that Bangladesh, under President Fakhrul’s leadership, would continue to make progress and advance the well-being of its people, according to the Pakistan High Commission in Dhaka.

The Pakistani President said Pakistan and Bangladesh enjoyed close bonds rooted in shared history, faith and cultural ties.

He welcomed the positive momentum in bilateral relations and expressed hope that cooperation between the two countries would continue to grow in areas of mutual interest.

Zardari said he looked forward to working with President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir to further strengthen Pakistan-Bangladesh relations and promote greater exchanges and cooperation between the peoples of the two countries.

The Pakistani President also invited President Fakhrul to visit Pakistan at a mutually convenient time.

He expressed confidence that the visit would provide an opportunity to further strengthen bilateral ties and deepen cooperation between Dhaka and Islamabad.

President Zardari also conveyed his best wishes to President Fakhrul for the successful discharge of his responsibilities and for the continued peace, progress and prosperity of the people of Bangladesh.

item.title: Moyeen Khan gets Local Govt, Partho Info, Millat Civil Aviation, Saching Prue CHT Affairs, two state ministers for Foreign Affairs
item.description:
The portfolios of the four newly sworn-in ministers and two state ministers have been allocated. At the same time, the portfolio of another minister has also been changed.

New President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir administered the oath to four ministers and two state ministers at Bangabhaban on Friday evening. First, Mirza Fakhrul Islam took oath as president. He then administered the oath to the new ministers and state ministers.

The four new ministers who took oath are Abdul Moyeen Khan, Rashiduzzaman Millat, Saching Prue Jeri and Andaleev Rahman Partho. Of them, Rashiduzzaman Millat had been serving as state minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism. The two new state ministers are Humayun Kabir (technocrat) and Mohammad Shamim Kaiser (Lincoln).

A high-level source at the Cabinet Division told Prothom Alo at night that the portfolios of the new ministers and state ministers had been allocated. A gazette notification will be issued shortly.

As Mirza Fakhrul Islam became president, Abdul Moyeen Khan has been given charge of the vacant Ministry of Local Government. Rashiduzzaman Millat, who took oath as a minister after serving as a state minister, has become the minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism. Afroza Khanam (Rita), who was the minister of this ministry, has been made minister for Food.

Saching Prue Jeri, a member of parliament from Bandarban, has been made minister for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs. After the BNP government took office, Dipen Dewan was given charge of the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs. However, he resigned after three months. Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin is currently serving as state minister for the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs.

Andaleev Rahman Partho, chairman of the BJP who took oath as a new minister, has been given charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Zahir Uddin Swapon, who had been serving as minister for the Information Ministry, has been made an adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

Shamim Kaiser has been given charge as state minister for the Ministry of Religious Affairs. Kazi Shah Mofazzal Hossain (Kaykobad) is the minister of this ministry.

New State Minister Humayun Kabir has been given charge as state minister for Foreign Affairs. Shama Obaed Islam, who was already serving as state minister for this ministry, will also remain in her previous post.

This means two state ministers will serve in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Khalilur Rahman is serving as the minister for Foreign Affairs.

item.title: Paredes suspended for 10 matches for World Cup fight, Argentina fined
item.description:
FILES-FBL-WC-2026-ARG-PAREDES-SUSPENSION

Argentina's Leandro Paredes received a 10-match suspension for his part in a brawl after his team lost to Spain in the World Cup final while teammate Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven games, FIFA announced on Friday.

A brief scuffle erupted at the final whistle when Argentina midfielder Paredes shoved Spain's Gavi to the ground as the European champions' substitutes rushed onto the pitch to celebrate.

Paredes faced three assault counts while Molina faced two. Both players were also fined $90,000 each.

Argentina’s Thiago Almada and Spain’s Gavi faced one count each of unsporting behaviour, while Argentina's assistant coach Roberto Ayala faced one assault count.

While Almada and Gavi received one-match suspensions, Ayala, who had apologised for his part in the altercation, was banned for three games, with all three fined $30,000.

The Argentinian Football Association (AFA) were fined a total of $321,000 for multiple disciplinary breaches during the World Cup, including the display by some players of a banner declaring "Las Malvinas Son Argentinas" ("The Falklands are Argentine") following their semi-final win over England.

The AFA was also ordered to play Argentina's next two home matches with spectators limited to 50 per cent of capacity.

FIFA had said using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature was a breach of the disciplinary code.

The fines were levied for breaches of the disciplinary code including use of a sports event for non-sporting demonstrations, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by fans.

"The FIFA Disciplinary Committee further determined that $100,000 of the $321,000 must be invested in a plan to combat discrimination," it said.

"The implementation of part of the sanction (one of the two matches and $100,000 of the fine) is suspended, with a probationary period to apply."

The decisions remain subject to appeal.

item.title: Cabinet reshuffle: Who is getting which ministry?
item.description:
The BNP-led government is set to make its first major cabinet reshuffle, with portfolios allocated to four newly appointed ministers and two state ministers, according to senior officials of the Cabinet Division.
The portfolio of another minister has also been changed, with a gazette notification expected to be issued by Friday night, the officials said.
On Friday evening, Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir took oath as the 23rd president of Bangladesh at Bangabhaban. He later administered the oath to four ministers and two state ministers.
The four new ministers are BNP Standing Committee member Abdul Moyeen Khan, Bangladesh Jatiya Party (BJP) Chairman Andaleeve Rahman Partho, former State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism Rashiduzzaman Millat, and Bandarban MP Saching Prue Jerry.
The two new state ministers are Prime Minister’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir and Gaibandha-4 MP Mohammad Shamim Kaiser Lincoln.
Abdul Moyeen Khan will take charge of the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, which was left vacant after Mirza Fakhrul became president.
Rashiduzzaman Millat, who has been elevated from state minister to minister, will head the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism. He had been serving as the state minister of the ministry.
The ministry’s current minister, Afroza Khanam (Rita), will be given another portfolio.
Saching Prue Jerry, a Bandarban MP and BNP Executive Committee member, will become the minister for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs.
Dipen Dewan had initially been appointed minister of the ministry after the BNP formed the government but later resigned. Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin is currently serving as its state minister.
Andaleeve Rahman Partho, chairman of the Bangladesh Jatiya Party (BJP), will take charge of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
Zahir Uddin Swapon, who has been serving as the minister of the ministry, will be appointed an adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman with ministerial rank.
Gaibandha-4 MP Mohammad Shamim Kaiser Lincoln will serve as state minister for Religious Affairs. Kazi Shah Mofazzal Hossain (Kaykobad) is the minister in charge of the ministry.
Humaiun Kobir will be appointed state minister for Foreign Affairs. Shama Obaed Islam is already serving as state minister at the ministry, meaning the Foreign Affairs Ministry will now have two state ministers.
Khalilur Rahman is serving as the foreign affairs minister.
The BNP formed the government under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on February 17 following its landslide victory in the 13th national parliamentary election.
Initially, 25 ministers and 24 state ministers took oath alongside the prime minister.
Later, Liberation War Affairs Minister Hafiz Uddin Ahmad and State Minister for Land Kaiser Kamal resigned after being elected speaker and deputy speaker, respectively.
Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs minister Dipen Dewan also subsequently resigned.
The Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Ministry was left vacant after Mirza Fakhrul won the presidential election and assumed office.
The vacancies and redistribution of portfolios have paved the way for the first major cabinet reshuffle of the BNP-led government.
The changes include the appointment of six new cabinet members, the transfer of Afroza Khanam’s portfolio and the appointment of Zahir Uddin Swapon as an adviser to the prime minister.

item.title: Humaiun Kobir: No country I can't speak to eye-to-eye
item.description:
Reiterating his commitment to safeguarding the country’s interests, newly appointed State Minister Humaiun Kobir on Friday night said that there is no country in the world with which he cannot speak “eye-to-eye” if he has the support of the people.
“Pray for me so that I am not compromised in any way. My belief is that there is no country in the world that I can not speak to eye-to-eye with if the people support us,” he told reporters soon after taking oath as state minister.
Kobir, who previously served as an Adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman before and after the formation of the government, said the new assignment reflects the prime minister’s confidence in him.
“I feel proud. It’s a new opportunity to work for the country. I will perform my responsibilities with the utmost sincerity and commitment, safeguarding the national interest,” Kobir said.
He said the position carries executive responsibilities and that he would fulfil his role with the utmost commitment, regardless of the portfolio assigned to him.
“Wherever I am placed, it’s a great opportunity to work for the government,” Kobir said.
He is expected to be appointed state minister for Foreign Affairs, even as State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam continues in her current role.

item.title: Lost in the jungle, claimed by heaven: Inside Allahr Masjid
item.description:
After driving for over two hours along the Dhaka-Barisal highway, I approached Torki, where my GPS signaled that Allahr Masjid was just ahead. The local betel leaf trade was in full, bustling swing as I arrived at Torki Bazar. This vibrant transit hub connects the Dhaka and Barisal divisions, sitting just past the Madaripur district border to mark one's entry into Gournadi, Barisal.
Moving a couple of kilometers further along National Highway-8, leaving Torki behind, I veered right and advanced a few yards. There, I was greeted by a 500-year-old, nine-domed mosque that locals call by a mysterious moniker: Allahr Masjid (God’s Mosque).
Located in Qasba village within Gournadi, this well-burnt red brick mosque features an adjoining courtyard and a calm, masonry-embanked pond. Believed to have been built in the early 16th century during the Bengal Sultanate period, the structure is alternately known as the Qasba Masjid.
This closer view highlights the signature architectural details of Allahr Masjid. The prominent circular brick column at the corner is a key defining feature of the Khan Jahan Ali style from the Bengal Sultanate period. Unlike free-standing Mughal minarets, these turrets are integrated into the main wall structure to provide both corner reinforcement and architectural symmetry. They typically extend slightly above the roofline and feature distinct horizontal brick moldings wrapping around the tower. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
I wondered why it was called Allahr Masjid in the first place.
According to oral folklore passed down through generations in Barisal, the mosque was not built by human hands. Local belief dictates that during the Mughal era—specifically during the reign of Emperor Jahangir—the area was blanketed by a dense jungle. When a group of workers cleared the forest for farming, they unexpectedly stumbled upon this beautiful, fully constructed brick mosque hidden beneath the overgrowth.
Because a massive, complete structure had emerged from the wilderness without a foundation plaque, stone inscription, or historical records, the local community could not attribute it to any specific king, saint, or builder.
Consequently, the locals decided that since only Allah knew its origin, it belonged directly to Him, thus naming it Allahr Masjid.
While legend attributes the structure to a miracle, architectural historians look at the mosque’s construction materials, curved cornices, and structural style to date it back to the early 16th-century Bengal Sultanate period. Some historical texts suggest it might have been commissioned by a local administrator named Sabi Khan during the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah (who ruled Bengal from 1494 to 1519). However, because his identity became obscure to the locals over the centuries, the supernatural name survived.
Such legends fascinate many visitors who come to see the historic mosque at Qasba. Yet, what amazed me more was the architectural beauty of this gem, widely celebrated as the oldest and most significant multi-domed Sultanate-era mosque in the entire Barisal Division.
The writer in front of the mosque with its wide front view, beautifully capturing the full scale of Allahr Masjid façade, highlighting its structural symmetry. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
It was around midday, and the Zohr prayer time was fast approaching. Since the Azan (call to prayer) had not yet sounded, I seized the opportunity to step into the prayer area inside the Qasba Masjid without causing any inconvenience to the musallis (congregants). Inside, I found four massive basalt stone pillars supporting a roof of nine domes. The interior space is divided into nine equal bays.
Though this old mosque remains an active place of worship today and is recognized as a protected archaeological monument by the Department of Archaeology, it is in need of some renovations. I noticed carpenters hammering loose planks and nails just to keep the old, weak, solid wood doors upright. This is not how we expect our heritage to decay.
Allahr Masjid features a square structure measuring 11.68 × 11.68 meters, with walls over two meters thick. Many people draw architectural similarities between Allahr Masjid and another nine-domed mosque in Bagerhat built by Khan Jahan Ali—a legendary 15th-century Sufi saint, administrator, and warrior who pioneered the development of southern Bengal. He is credited with introducing a unique architectural movement to South Asia. Buildings in this style feature solid brick masonry, gently curved cornices, circular corner towers, and low-lying, unadorned domes designed to withstand heavy delta rains.
The single-story mosque’s stone pillars culminate in stone brackets, from which brick arches spring upward to form the squinches holding up the domes. It features three arched entrances on the eastern facade, with the central entrance being slightly larger. There are also single arched doorways on both the north and south walls for cross-ventilation.
A dighi (large pond) located right next to the Allahr Masjid complex. Large ponds like this are an integral feature of ancient Bengal Sultanate and Mughal-era Islamic complexes. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The exterior consists of exposed, well-burnt red bricks laid with lime and brick-dust mortar, giving it a distinct, rustic red color. The facades, particularly around the arched openings and the Mihrab , are decorated with subtle terracotta relief panels. Mihrab serves as where the imam (prayer leader) stands to guide the congregation. These feature traditional geometric patterns, hanging chain motifs, and stylized floral designs that strictly avoid living figures in adherence to Islamic tradition.
As I left the mosque complex and its adjoining pond, I walked a few yards down a herringbone-patterned brick road lined with trees. Before rolling back onto the Barisal highway, I looked back; the radiant red-brick color of Allahr Masjid was still peeking beautifully through the dense green foliage.

item.description:
The Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police recovered the motorcycle used in the sensational Tk1.21 crore robbery at a filling station in the capital's Uttara area on Friday noon.
Detectives recovered the Pulsar motorcycle around 10:30pm on Thursday from a building garage on Hafiz Uddin Master Road in the Nandipara area of Khilgaon, following information extracted from arrested suspect Sagar Barai during remand interrogation.
Md Elias Kabir, deputy commissioner of DB Uttara Division, said the DB has prioritized the investigation into the high-profile robbery since its occurrence. As part of ongoing operations, law enforcers have conducted raids across various areas in Dhaka and Narayanganj, arresting five suspects, including Sagar Barai.
Police also seized four firearms, a portion of the looted cash, and other crucial evidence from the possession of the arrestees. Drives are currently ongoing to apprehend the remaining suspects and recover the rest of the weapons used during the heist, officials added.

Amir Khosru: Higher education must be linked to employment, entrepreneurship
item.description:
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury on Friday called for linking higher education with employment and entrepreneurship, urging authorities to consider priority sectors, employment prospects and entrepreneurial opportunities while establishing new universities and introducing new faculties and subjects.
“Higher education subjects and curricula must be determined in line with the country’s economic needs and labour market realities. The goal of higher education should not be limited to obtaining certificates; it should also prepare students for employment and entrepreneurship,” he said.
The minister was addressing the ‘Vice-Chancellors' Dialogue: Shaping the Future of Higher Education’, a two-day national policy dialogue organised under the Higher Education Acceleration and Transformation (HEAT) Project of the University Grants Commission (UGC) at BRAC CDM in Savar.
He also stressed the need for stronger university-industry collaboration, saying universities and industries in many countries maintain close links and Bangladesh should utilise the potential of such cooperation.
“Why can’t we develop industry-university interaction in Bangladesh? Around the world, universities and industries are seriously connected. We need to utilise this potential,” he said.
Amir Khosru said international and national rankings of higher education institutions have an impact not only on employment opportunities and global recognition but also on the overall image of a country.
He urged universities to identify the reasons behind the weak university-industry linkage and the mismatch between education and labour market requirements.
“Why can’t we change our education system in relation to the job market?” he asked, stressing the need to establish a stronger relationship between education and employment.
The minister also underscored the importance of research as a fundamental component of higher education and called for linking research with industry.
“Research is fundamental for education. We need to determine our priorities in research and explore how we can connect research with industry,” he said.
He urged universities to conduct research to address real-life problems faced by industries and businesses and called upon the private sector to finance university research and commercially utilise research findings.
“Research should not remain confined to publications; it must contribute to national development and people’s welfare,” he said.
Questioning the academic structure of newly established universities, Amir Khosru said their faculties and academic programmes should be selected based on specific educational, regional and employment needs.
“I do not know under what consideration these faculties have been selected. I don’t see the reason,” he said. He said establishing new universities was a positive development, but their academic programmes should be designed to address the needs of the regions where they are located.
“What target are we trying to fulfil through these universities? Do people in those areas have proper opportunities to enter the job market?” he asked.
He said newly established universities have an advantage as they could be designed from the beginning to address existing challenges in higher education.
The minister said he would request the UGC to formulate appropriate guidelines on the faculties and subjects to be introduced at newly established universities, taking into account regional needs, priority sectors and employment opportunities.

item.title: Centuries-old temple set for restoration in Satkhira
item.description:
The historic Shyamsundar Temple at Sonabaria village in Kalaroa upazila of Satkhira is finally set to receive long-awaited conservation attention, with Department of Archaeology preparing to undertake scientific documentation before launching full-scale restoration.
The development follows a series of media reports highlighting the temple’s deteriorating condition and urging authorities to take immediate steps to preserve the heritage site. A team from Department of Archaeology’s Khulna regional office inspected the temple on Wednesday as part of preparations for its conservation.
During the visit, the officials and experts examined the temple’s structural condition, walls, cornices, terracotta decorations and other deteriorated sections. They also discussed the technical and scientific measures required before restoration begins.
Mahidul Islam, regional director of Department of Archaeology, said the Shyamsundar Temple is an important antiquity listed in the government gazette. “Initial cleaning has already been completed. Pre-documentation is essential before starting the main restoration work to ensure that no part of the structure’s original form or heritage value is damaged,” he said.
He said a team of experts would carry out detailed scientific documentation, including architectural drawings, measurements and other necessary data collection. Full-scale restoration would begin after the documentation is completed.
Necessary allocation would be sought in the next fiscal year for permanent restoration and conservation of the temple, he said, adding that old trees and parasitic plants growing on the structure would be removed carefully and gradually to prevent damage to the historic fabric of the building.
Shapla Singha, Assistant Professor at Khulna University, said that preserving the temple should involve more than restoring its physical structure. She said the history and cultural practices associated with the site should also be documented and preserved.
She also suggested using dioramas or photographic displays to recreate the atmosphere of the site during the pre-electricity era, particularly how the temple and its surroundings appeared at night. Such an initiative, she said, could serve as a model for preserving other historic temples and mosques in Bangladesh.
Temple president Debapriya Chowdhury and priest Subroprosad Chowdhury welcomed the initiative, saying the historic site had long suffered from neglect and disturbances caused by drug users. They urged the authorities to construct a boundary wall as soon as possible to ensure the security and sanctity of the temple.
According to historian Satish Chandra Mitra and Professor Md Abu Nasr, the nearly 60-foot-high, three-storey Shyamsundar Temple was built in 1767 by Hariram Das, although some accounts identify the builder as Durgapriya Das. The temple complex also includes shrines dedicated to Durga and Shiva and a historic pond known as “Jamir Biswaser Pukur.”
With Department of Archaeology now moving ahead with scientific pre-documentation and promising restoration funding in the next fiscal year, hopes are growing that the centuries-old temple will finally be preserved and developed as an important heritage and tourism destination in southwestern Bangladesh.

item.title: Helping the youth help the nation
item.description:
The call for Bangladesh’s youth to pursue skill development with national interests in mind is both timely and necessary.
As the country faces a rapidly changing global economy, technological disruption, and an increasingly competitive international labour market, young people cannot afford to remain confined to conventional career paths.
Their skills must, therefore, be relevant to emerging industries, changing market demands, and the broader needs of the economy.
However, the responsibility for building a productive, skilled, and socially conscious youth population cannot rest on young people alone.
If the state expects the youth to work for the national interest, then the nation and the state must reciprocate by creating an environment in which young people can actually realize their potential.
As the minister rightly pointed out, training people for existing jobs is insufficient; Bangladesh must also create new employment opportunities and expand the market itself.
This requires coherent industrial policies, investment in emerging sectors, easier access to finance for entrepreneurs, stronger infrastructure, and an education and training system that responds to actual market needs.
Most importantly, skills development must lead somewhere; it is unfair to repeatedly urge young people to become more employable when decent employment remains scarce, wages fail to reflect skills, and opportunities are concentrated in a limited number of sectors.
A skilled generation without adequate avenues to apply those skills represents not only individual frustration but also a significant loss of national potential.
The example of policy support that helped lay the foundations of Bangladesh’s garment industry demonstrates what can happen when human capital development is matched with appropriate state intervention.
Our youth should certainly recognize their responsibility to the country, but the country must also recognize its responsibility to them.
Bangladesh’s young people are among its most valuable drivers. If we expect them to build the nation, we must give them the tools, opportunities, and institutional support to do so.

item.title: Redefining the president’s role
item.description:
Bangladesh welcomes Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as its new president. Congratulations are in order for a man who fully deserves this honour after decades of public service.
His election -- the first genuinely contested presidential vote in decades -- marks an important democratic moment for our country as we continue to try and bring back democratic ideals that were all but lost in our recent history.
With that said, we must remember that Mirza Fakhrul now assumes the nation’s highest constitutional office and thus, invites a necessary conversation about what the presidency has been in Bangladesh, and what it could become.
For much of this country’s history, the presidency has been treated as largely ceremonial. Indeed, that the president has been confined to formal duties such as issuing messages, attending state functions, and performing the rituals of office is not all a president of a nation should be reduced to.
This is a role that carries immense symbolic weight, being the only office meant to stand above partisanship and representing the republic rather than any single political interest. This is key for a nation that looks to have only become more politically polarized over the years.
Bangladesh today faces institutional challenges that demand steady national leadership. The presidency can -- and should -- play a more meaningful part in shaping our democratic culture.
Given Mirza Fakhrul’s long history in politics and his involvement with Bangladesh ever since its inception, he has the pedigree to speak when others cannot, urge restraint when tensions rise, and elevate issues that require long‑term national attention.
The question now is whether he will be empowered and encouraged to do so. Bangladesh, however, would benefit from a president who is more active in its nation-building endeavours.
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir now has the opportunity to redefine expectations. We congratulate him, and hope his role is allowed to be not just ceremonial, but genuinely impactful for the betterment of our nation.

item.title: A warning we cannot afford to ignore
item.description:
The Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination has long been regarded as a major academic milestone in Bangladesh -- a high-stakes examination that shapes students' academic and career prospects. Yet, the high failure rate in this year's SSC results has raised serious concerns among educators, families, and policy-makers.
The poor performance in core subjects, particularly English and Mathematics, is troubling. It might be tempting to dismiss the results as an isolated setback or a sign of declining student capability, but doing so would be a mistake.
Instead, these outcomes should be recognized as a warning sign of systemic weaknesses within our education system.
If Bangladesh is serious about building the human capital required for a competitive, technology-driven economy, it must look past mere examination results and confront the roots of learning deficits. The core issue is not simply why so many students failed this year, but why the education system has allowed them to reach the SSC level without acquiring the essential knowledge and competencies for success.
The SSC crisis reflects unaddressed learning gaps originating in primary school and widening through secondary education. Burdened by a high-stress curriculum, students with foundational weaknesses in core subjects -- such as English, math, and analytical reasoning -- inevitably struggle as coursework grows more complex.
Without early intervention, the system advances students who lack basic competencies. Viewed in this light, an SSC failure is not a sudden mishap, but the visible symptom of a multi-year learning deficit.
For decades, much of our education system has placed excessive emphasis on rote memorization, examination scores, and GPA-5s rather than genuine comprehension. Students are encouraged to reproduce textbook material instead of analyzing, questioning, applying, and problem-solving.
This approach has fostered a dependence on guidebooks, model answers, and strictly examination-oriented preparation. Consequently, when assessments demand conceptual understanding rather than predictable recall, many students struggle.
The core issue is not simply that students cannot answer difficult questions; it is that the system has consistently failed to teach them how to think critically.
Schools are not just places for learning from textbooks. They are also important centers for children’s physical, mental, social, and moral development.
At the primary level, children need to develop essential life skills such as social interaction, emotional control, communication, creativity, and cooperation. At the secondary level, these should be strengthened with skills such as problem-solving, critical thinking, effective communication, digital literacy, and leadership.
The goal of education, therefore, should not be limited to getting good marks in examinations; it should also prepare students for life and the world of work.
Compounding this is the systemic concern surrounding fairness and transparency in teacher recruitment. Because teachers play a vital role in properly guiding students during their foundational years, addressing deployment policies and continuous professional development remains an urgent priority.
Many institutions, particularly outside major urban centers, face severe shortages of qualified educators in critical subjects. However, merely recruiting qualified teachers is insufficient.
To foster a thriving learning environment, educators also require ongoing professional development, meaningful evaluation frameworks, and robust career support.
Education reform must therefore address the entire teacher life-cycle -- from recruitment and induction to training and professional accountability.
Another neglected issue is the disruption of academic activities in schools. Political unrest, student conflicts, institutional disputes, and administrative challenges frequently reduce instructional time while undermining attendance and learning continuity.
Educational institutions must remain sanctuaries for learning, intellectual development, and academic freedom. To achieve this, the government and political parties must forge a consensus to keep schools and universities entirely free from organized partisan politics and political interference.
A substantial disparity persists between well-resourced institutions in major cities and schools in rural or disadvantaged areas. While urban institutions typically enjoy access to qualified teachers, modern laboratories, and digital infrastructure, rural institutions often struggle with chronic teacher shortages and inadequate facilities.
Consequently, public investment must prioritize institutions where educational resources are weakest.
The proliferation of coaching centers and private tutoring is both a symptom and a consequence of systemic weaknesses in mainstream education. When students and parents lose faith in classroom instruction, they naturally turn to external alternatives.
However, commercial coaching prioritizes exam-oriented tactics over true comprehension. Moreover, excessive reliance on private tutoring exacerbates inequality, as affluent families can easily afford supplemental academic support.
Ultimately, the definitive solution lies in restoring public confidence in mainstream classroom teaching.
Education policy should transcend shifting political cycles. Bangladesh requires a stable, long-term national framework rooted in evidence and broad consultation.
To achieve this, a permanent, independent National Education Commission -- comprising educators, researchers, and stakeholders -- should be established to periodically review curricula, assessments, and teacher development.
A core mandate of the Commission should be steering the education system toward outcome- or competency-based education (OBE/CBE) from primary school to higher education. By drawing on successful regional models, such as India’s National Education Policy 2020 and reforms in Malaysia, Bangladesh can align its teaching and assessment standards with clear, measurable competencies suited to its own context.
Assessment must measure whether students have mastered expected competencies rather than merely testing their capacity to reproduce memorized material.
Policy-makers and educators must prioritize conceptual understanding, analytical ability, problem-solving, effective communication, and the practical application of knowledge. While continuous or school-based assessment can play a valuable role, it requires robust moderation and rigorous quality assurance to prevent grade inflation.
Recent SSC results serve as a stark reminder that educational quality cannot be measured by pass rates alone. A high pass rate does not guarantee meaningful learning, just as a low pass rate does not place the blame for poor performance solely on students.
While Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in expanding educational access, the next critical challenge is ensuring true comprehension -- cultivating young people equipped to think critically, solve problems, communicate effectively, and leverage technology intelligently.
Consequently, these results should not be dismissed as an isolated setback, but rather seized as an opportunity to confront systemic weaknesses and enact lasting reforms.
MM Shahidul Hassan is a distinguished professor at Eastern University, and former Vice Chancellor of East West University, Bangladesh.

item.title: When hope travels, so does exploitation
item.description:
"I crossed the border without documents or a passport. A friend I met through social media promised me a better-paying job at a beauty parlour. I believed I was chasing a better future. Instead, I was sexually exploited and eventually ended up in jail."
She shared these words with me shortly after she was repatriated to Dhaka.
What stayed with me was not only her story, but also the question she asked before we parted.
"If someone had told me what could happen, would my life have been different?"
I have returned to that question many times since.
Over the years, through my work with returnee migrants and survivors of trafficking and exploitative migration, I have listened to many stories of journeys that ended very differently from how they began.
Yet the experiences of women have stayed with me the most. Their stories are not simply about migration gone wrong. They reveal how hope can become a pathway to exploitation when it is shaped by misinformation, unequal power, and limited choices.
Months later, I met another woman whose story unsettled me in a different way. She had travelled to Saudi Arabia believing she had secured a job as a domestic worker. Instead, she was subjected to repeated sexual violence. Even the person she trusted to help her escape exploited her further.
When she eventually returned to Bangladesh, she was pregnant as a result of that abuse. Yet what struck me was not only the violence she endured abroad, but also what awaited her at home. Instead of finding comfort, she found silence and rejection. Her family struggled to accept both her and her child.
The two women had never met. Their journeys followed different routes and ended in different countries. Yet their stories began in remarkably similar ways.
Someone they trusted promised them a better future.
Listening to these women changed how I understand labour migration. Before meeting them, I often thought about trafficking and labour exploitation as crimes committed by traffickers or abusive employers. Their stories challenged that assumption.
Neither woman intended to become an irregular migrant or a survivor of exploitation. Both believed they were making responsible decisions for themselves and their families. Their journeys began not with criminal intent, but with trust.
As I reflected on their experiences, I realized I had been asking the wrong question. I had been asking how exploitation happens. They led me to ask why so many women are placed in situations where exploitation becomes possible in the first place.
Sociologists have long argued that migration is shaped by the interaction between individual aspirations and the broader social and economic structures that shape people's choices. People migrate because opportunities at home are limited while possibilities elsewhere appear within reach.
Yet contemporary research reminds us that exploitation rarely begins with violence. It emerges where poverty, gender inequality, deceptive recruitment, limited information, and unequal power converge. By the time exploitation becomes visible, vulnerability has often been building long before a woman boards a plane or crosses a border.
The first woman did not cross the border because she wanted to take unnecessary risks. She crossed because someone convinced her the risks were small. The second woman did not leave believing she would be abused. She left believing she had secured legitimate employment.
What failed them was not simply their judgement. It was the system of trust surrounding their decisions.
That trust is easy to understand.
Across Bangladesh, labour migration has become part of many families' aspirations. A neighbour returns with a newly built house. A relative pays for a child's education through overseas earnings. A family escapes debt because someone found work abroad. These stories travel quickly through communities, quietly shaping the belief that migration is the surest path to a better life.
The stories that travel less often are those of women who return carrying trauma instead of opportunity.
Many of the women I have spoken with could clearly remember the salaries they had been promised. Few, however, knew much about their employment contracts, their rights in the destination country, or where they could seek help if something went wrong.
Some relied entirely on verbal assurances from brokers or acquaintances. Others believed paperwork could be completed after arrival. None imagined that the very people they trusted could become part of the danger.
Whenever I meet returnee migrants now, I find myself listening differently. I no longer hear only where they travelled or how they returned. I listen for the moment when hope first became vulnerability.
Women often face additional risks because many migrate into domestic work, where employment takes place inside private homes. Unlike most workplaces, these environments remain largely hidden from public oversight, making abuse, sexual violence, wage theft, and restrictions on movement far more difficult to detect or report.
When exploitation occurs, seeking help can itself become another source of vulnerability, as the second woman's experience painfully demonstrated.
Yet the challenges rarely end when women return home.
For many survivors, the violence they experienced abroad is followed by silence, stigma, and social rejection. Reintegration becomes more than finding employment again. It becomes the struggle to rebuild dignity, relationships, and a sense of belonging.
The woman I met at the border asked whether someone could have changed her future simply by telling her the truth.
The more I reflect on her question, the less I believe it is only about information.
It is about responsibility.
Families are often the first people a woman turns to before deciding to migrate. Asking difficult questions before encouraging that decision may be just as important as celebrating the opportunity itself.
Is the recruiter licensed? Has the employment contract been verified? Does she understand her rights? Does she know where to seek help if something goes wrong? These conversations may not eliminate every risk, but they can help women make informed choices.
The government has an equally important responsibility. Safer migration requires stronger oversight of recruitment practices, transparent migration processes, accessible information, gender-responsive pre-departure orientation, effective protection through Bangladeshi missions abroad, and survivor-centred reintegration that recognizes recovery as more than an economic process.
Protection should accompany women throughout the migration journey, not begin only after exploitation has occurred.
I often find myself returning to the question the first woman asked me.
"If someone had told me what could happen, would my life have been different?"
Perhaps that question should no longer belong only to her. It should belong to every family deciding whether to send a daughter abroad. It should belong to every recruiter whose promises influence life-changing decisions. It should belong to policy-makers responsible for protecting migrant workers. And it should belong to all of us who celebrate migration's economic contributions while too rarely listening to those whose journeys ended differently.
Her question cannot change the past. But it can shape the future.
If it encourages one family to ask harder questions, one woman to seek reliable information before leaving home, or one institution to strengthen protection before another journey begins, then perhaps fewer women will one day have to ask it at all.
Md Shihabul Hossain is deputy manager, migration program, Brac.

item.title: Starc takes five wickets as Bangladesh 35 for six at lunch
item.description:
Australia paceman Mitchell Starc took five wickets in 22 balls in a brilliant spell of quick bowling as Bangladesh staggered to lunch at 35 for six on day one of the second test in Mackay, Queensland on Saturday.

  • Starc's was the sixth-fastest five-wicket haul in tests. The left-hander holds the record for the fastest, having taken five wickets in 15 balls against West Indies in Kingston last year.

  • Bangladesh all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz was 11 not out, with number eight Hasan Mahmud on eight at the break.

  • Starc removed both Bangladesh openers, captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and wicketkeeper Litton Das for ducks to leave the tourists at 12 for five, after Australia captain Pat Cummins won the toss and elected to field.

  • Opener Shadman Islam was out with the first ball of the match after sending a thick edge flying to Cameron Green in the gully.

  • Opener Tanzid Hasan followed in Starc's next over with a loose drive sending a nick to Beau Webster in the slips, before Shanto was trapped lbw on the next ball, leaving Bangladesh at 9 for three.

  • Starc grabbed his fourth wicket when number three Mominul Haque drove at a full, wider delivery, nicking to Green at the gully. He took his fifth with another lbw to remove Das.

  • Cummins bowled Bangladesh number five Mushfiqur Rahim for five on a bouncy pitch likened to a typical Gabba wicket.

  • Bangladesh lead the series 1-0 after a nine-wicket win in the series-opener in Darwin.

  • Matt Renshaw to open the batting for Australia in his first test in over three years, with Jake Weatherald dropped after consecutive failures in Darwin.

  • Bangladesh made one change to their Darwin XI, bringing in left-arm paceman Shoriful Islam after his recovery from a hamstring injury. He replaced fellow quick Ebadot Hossain.

  • Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena became Australia's 12th test venue.

item.title: Cabinet reshuffle: Gazette issued, who gets which ministry
item.description:
The government has issued a gazette allocating portfolios to four new ministers and two state ministers and reshuffling the portfolio of another minister.

The Cabinet Division issued the gazette notification, signed by Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani on Friday night.

According to the gazette, issued under Rule 3(4) of the Rules of Business, 1996, the Prime Minister has allocated and reallocated ministerial portfolios as follows:

BNP Standing Committee member Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan has been assigned the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives; Rashiduzzaman Millat MP, the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism; Lawmaker from Bandarban Saching Prue Jerry, the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs and Chairman of Bangladesh National Party (BJP) Andaleeve Rahman Partho, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

Afroza Khanam Rita, who was previously in charge of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism, has been assigned the Ministry of Food.

Among the state ministers, Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir has been given charge of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs while Gaibandha-4 lawmaker Mohammad Shamim Kaiser Lincoln has been assigned the Ministry of Religious Affairs.

The gazette said all other matters contained in the gazettes issued on 17 February, 4 March, 12 March and 25 March will remain unchanged.

The order will take effect immediately, it added.

item.title: Starc finishes with six as Bangladesh all out for 64 in first innings of second test v Australia
item.description:
A rampant Australia tore through the Bangladesh batting Saturday to dismiss them for just 64 on day one of the second Test with Mitchell Starc taking 6-12 after a bowling masterclass.

Skipper Pat Cummins won the toss in Mackay and his bowlers feasted on a fine day, determined to bounce back from a shock nine-wicket loss in the first Test at Darwin.

An irrepressible Starc was the destroyer in an incredible spell of swing and seam, taking five wickets in just 22 balls during the morning session to leave the visitors on the ropes.

Bangladesh reached lunch at 35-6 and lasted barely an hour after the break as Starc, Cummins and Josh Hazlewood mopped up the tail.

Only a last-wicket partnership of 25 between Taijul Islam (not out 11) and Shoriful Islam (14) took them past their lowest Test score of 43, against the West Indies in 2018.

Australia made a stunning start when Starc removed Shadman Islam with the first ball of the day, tempting a leading edge that Cameron Green did well to hold in the gully.

It was the fourth time the veteran left-armer has got a wicket with the maiden ball of a Test -- becoming the first player to do so -- and the ninth time he has achieved the feat in the opening over.

The 36-year-old sent Bangladesh's other opener Tanzid Hasan packing with the first ball of his second over, caught at slip by Beau Webster, then trapped captain Najmul Hossain Shanto lbw with his next delivery.

It left the visitors reeling at 3-9 in the third over.

The experienced Mushfiqur Rahim fended off Starc's hat-trick ball, but he was unstoppable and grabbed his fourth wicket in his third over.

This time, Mominul Haque was the victim in a similar dismissal to Shadman, undone by late swing to send a thick edge low to Green in the gully on nine.

Webster dropped a sitter at third slip off Starc in his fourth over, but Litton Das' luck ran out next ball, out lbw on review as the visitors slumped to 5-12.

It was the 19th time Starc has taken five wickets in an innings and achieved in just 22 balls -- the sixth fastest of all-time.

Starc holds the record after taking five in only 15 balls in Jamaica against the West Indies in 2025.

Mushfiqur hung around for 41 balls but he had no answer when Cummins came on, clean bowled for five.

Cummins struck again in his first over after lunch to dismiss Mehidy Hasan Miraz for 11, taken brilliantly by Webster in the slips, before Hazlewood took care of Hasan Mahmud (10) eight balls later.

Bangladesh moved past their previous lowest score in Tests as the tailenders hit out, but the end was inevitable with Starc fittingly wrapping it up with the wicket of Shoriful.

item.title: Chhayanaut echoes with Tagore’s timeless melodies
item.description:
“Shakatore oi kandiche shokole”—the two-day commemoration marking the 85th death anniversary of Rabindranath Tagore began with a chorus performance of one of the poet’s songs, as artists brought his timeless works to life through music.
The program, featuring songs exploring themes of separation, love, nature and the human spirit, began on Friday at Chhayanaut in the capital, organised by the Bangladesh Rabindra Sangeet Shilpi Sangstha.
The opening chorus was followed by “Aguner Poroshmoni Chhoyao Prane, E Jibon Purno Koro,” setting the tone for an evening dedicated to Tagore’s music.
Ahmad Maya Akhtari then took the stage for a solo performance.
A number of Rabindra Sangeet artistes subsequently performed throughout the evening, including Anushree Bhattacharya, Suchitra Chakraborty, Sumana Das, Talat Sultana, Kushal Roy Joy, Tanushree Deepak, Moumita Momi, Sharmila Chakraborty, Shakil Hashmi, Shilpi Saha, Zeenat Ferdous Chobi, Bandana Rani Gomsta, Sushmit Saif Islam, Sumi Chakraborty, Sabrina Rahman, Ankhi Halder, Bulbul Islam, Tanushree Bhattacharya, Zafar Ahmed, Smritikana Pal and Liton Chandra Vaidya.
Anushree Bhattacharya performed “Jani Jani Tumi Eshocho Ei Pothe”, while Suchitra Chakraborty presented “Oi Shuni Jaan Charan Dhwani Re”. Sumana Das performed “Mam Mon Upobone” and Talat Sultana sang “Sokarun Benu Bajaye Ke Jaye”.
Kushal Roy Joy performed “Amar Ja Ache Ami Sakal Dite Parini Tomar Name”, followed by Tanushree Deepak’s “Utal Dhara Badol Jhore Sakal Bela”. Moumita Momi presented “Agnibeena Bajao Tumi”, while Sharmila Chakraborty performed “Shondhya Holo Go Ma”.
The main auditorium of Chhayanaut remained filled with Tagore’s songs as the performances continued.
Shakil Hashmi performed “Chinile Na Amare Ki”, while Shilpi Saha sang “Tomar Mohon Rupe Ke Roy Bhule”. Zeenat Ferdous presented “Ya Pakhtan Pakhtan Pyar Pakhtan”.
Bandana Rani Gomsta performed “Bhubon Jora Asonkhani”, followed by Sushmit Saif Islam’s “Shokti Rupe Heroh Tare”. Sumi Chakraborty sang “Barish Dhara Majhe Shantir Bari”, while Sabrina Rahman performed “Tumi Ektu Keboli Boshte Diyo Kachhe”.
Ankhi Halder’s rendition of “Megher Pore Megh Jomechhe, Andhar Ghonie Ashe” created a different mood, followed by Bulbul Islam’s “Pothe Jete Jete Tomar Porosh Ashe”.
Tanushree Bhattacharya then performed “Dekho Dekho Dekho Shuktara Ankhi Mele Chay”.
Smritikana Pal sang “Tomarei Koriyechi Jibon Dhrubatara”, while Liton Chandra Vaidya concluded the solo performances with “Aji Pranam Tomare Chholib Na”.
At the beginning of the program, Bangladesh Rabindra Sangeet Shilpi Sangstha General Secretary Piyush Barua welcomed the audience.
“This is our program marking the 85th death anniversary of Rabindranath Tagore. On behalf of our organisation, I express my sincere gratitude and thanks to everyone who has joined us,” he said.
He added that the organisation’s President Tapan Mahmud and Executive President Amina Ahmed were currently abroad.
“They are not with us at the moment, so we are organising the programme largely without their guidance. I hope you will join us tomorrow and encourage our artists,” Piyush Barua said.
Acting President of the Bangladesh Rabindra Sangeet Shilpi Sangstha, artist Khandaker Khairuzzaman Qayyum, formally opened the programme by greeting the audience.
The first day of the two-day commemoration was more than a formal tribute to Tagore. Through a succession of his songs performed by different artists, the evening offered the audience an opportunity to revisit the poet’s works and connect with his music in a renewed way.

item.title: Gold price rises by Tk 5,482 per bhori in one go
item.description:
The price of gold has increased in the domestic market following a rise in prices in the global market. The price of good-quality, or 22-carat, gold has increased by Tk 5,482 per bhori today, Saturday.

The new price came into effect at 10am today, Saturday. The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (BAJUS), the organisation of gold traders, announced the decision to increase the price in a notice at 10:00 am today.

BAJUS said the new prices were adjusted due to a rise in the price of tezaabi gold in the local market.

Although the organisation cited the rise in the price of tezaabi gold in the local market as the reason for the increase, the decision was mainly driven by the rise in gold prices in the global market.

Following the latest increase, the price of one bhori of 22-carat gold, considered good quality, has risen to Tk 246,110 from today; 21-carat gold to Tk 235,030; 18-carat gold to Tk 201,845; and gold under the traditional method to Tk 164,812.

Before today’s increase, the price of gold was as follows: 22-carat gold was Tk 240,628 per bhori; 21-carat gold Tk 229,781; 18-carat gold Tk 197,355; and gold under the traditional method Tk 161,196.

Earlier, the price of gold was increased on 20 August. On that day, the price rose by a maximum of Tk 3,849 per bhori.

The highest-ever price of gold in the domestic market was Tk 286,000. On January 29 this year, the price of gold reached an all-time high in the country. That morning, the price jumped by Tk 16,213 per bhori to Tk 286,000.

Meanwhile, the price of silver has also increased alongside gold. The price of good-quality, or 22-carat, silver has increased by Tk 175 per bhori.

As a result, the price of one bhori of silver has risen to Tk 5,482 from today, Thursday. The price of 21-carat silver has increased to Tk 5,249 per bhori.

item.title: Australia lose 3 wickets in reply to Bangladesh's 64 in second test
item.description:
Australia were 50 for three at tea on day one of the second test against Bangladesh in reply to the tourists' first-innings total of 64 in Mackay, Queensland on Saturday.

Steve Smith was six not out, with Cameron Green on one. Bangladesh's lead was down to 14 runs by the break.

Recalled paceman Shoriful Islam took two quick wickets late in the session, bowling opener Travis Head for 22 and out-of-form number three Marnus Labuschagne for four.

Taskin Ahmed had the recalled opener Matt Renshaw caught for eight in the slips.

Bangladesh were bowled out after lunch, after Australia captain Pat Cummins won the toss and elected to field on a bouncy wicket prepared like a typical Gabba pitch.

Australia paceman Mitchell Starc took five wickets in 22 balls. The left-armer finished with 6-12 after completing the sixth-fastest five-wicket haul in tests. Starc holds the record for the fastest (15 balls) against West Indies in Kingston last year.

Starc struck with the first ball of the match to remove opener Shadman Islam and captured the first five wickets, leaving the tourists reeling at 12 for five after 6.4 overs. He returned to have tailender Shoriful caught behind for 14 to wrap up the innings.

Apart from Shadman, opener Tanzid Hasan, captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and wicketkeeper Litton Das all fell for ducks off Starc's bowling.

Shadman was caught in the gully after sending a thick edge flying to Cameron Green. Tanzid Hasan drove loosely at a fuller ball to nick to Beau Webster in the slips, while Shanto was trapped lbw on the next ball.

Number three Mominul Haque managed nine runs before nicking to Green at gully with another loose drive at a wider Starc delivery. Starc grabbed his fifth wicket with another lbw to remove Das.

Cummins finished with 3-25. He bowled Bangladesh number five Mushfiqur Rahim for five and had all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz caught in the slips for 11. The home captain also had tailender Taskin caught for one at square leg. Josh Hazlewood chipped in with the wicket of Hasan Mahmud for 10.

Bangladesh lead the series 1-0 after a nine-wicket win in the series-opener in Darwin.

Renshaw was recalled for his first test in over three years, replacing the dropped Jake Weatherald.

Bangladesh made one change to their Darwin XI, bringing in Shoriful after his recovery from a hamstring injury. He replaced fellow quick Ebadot Hossain.

Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena became Australia's 12th test venue.

item.title: Sudden announcement by India’s Rashtrapati Bhavan sparks surprise, speculation
item.description:
Has Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India become uncertain? If not, why would the Rashtrapati Bhavan make such an announcement, only to withdraw it within an hour? This was the subject of intense speculation on Friday afternoon. However, the reason behind the Rashtrapati Bhavan’s announcement remained shrouded in mystery.

The diplomatic circles of both countries have been abuzz for several days over Tarique Rahman’s possible visit to India. At one point, it was thought that Tarique Rahman would visit India on a bilateral trip before attending the BRICS summit’s outreach session as chairman of BIMSTEC.

Just as that possibility was gaining momentum, the Bangladesh government raised serious questions about the conduct of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who is staying in India after being convicted. Bangladesh also sought certain assurances or imposed conditions regarding Hasina’s future conduct while staying in India.

Since then, speculation surrounding Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit had subsided. Against this backdrop, the Rashtrapati Bhavan announcement came at around 2:00 pm on Friday, followed shortly afterwards by a statement from the Press Information Bureau (PIB).

Navika Gupta, deputy press secretary to the President, issued a press release at 2:13 pm saying that the ‘Change of Guard’ ceremony would not be held at the Rashtrapati Bhavan on Saturday.

The reason given was that a full rehearsal would be held at that time for a ceremonial reception for the Prime Minister of Bangladesh. The Rashtrapati Bhavan’s announcement was also circulated by the PIB shortly afterwards. This triggered fresh speculation over the stalled visit.

The media immediately became active. Questions were repeatedly raised with the Ministry of External Affairs on the matter. Was Tarique Rahman coming after all? After some time, the Ministry of External Affairs said the announcement was incorrect.

The statement was removed from the PIB website. At 3:32pm, Navika Gupta also announced that the earlier statement had been withdrawn. Although it became clear that someone had made a mistake, the identity of the person responsible and how such a mistake occurred remained a mystery.

According to various sources, Tarique Rahman’s visit to India had been considered final. The belief became stronger following Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi’s visit to Delhi.

Accordingly, a decision had been taken to cancel the ‘Change of Guard’ ceremony at the Rashtrapati Bhavan on Saturday, 22 August. A dinner at Hyderabad House on 24 August had also reportedly been confirmed. It is being heard that invitations had even been sent to many people. However, there has been no official confirmation of these reports.

Still, the question remains: How could such a major mistake have occurred? Who is responsible for it? There is no answer to these questions in any quarter. The ‘Change of Guard’ ceremony at the Rashtrapati Bhavan is a longstanding military tradition. The ceremony takes place every Saturday morning, when the old guards responsible for the President’s security hand over their duties to a new guard contingent and leave.

The visually impressive military ceremony features a cavalry parade and the sound of a military band. Tickets for the ceremony are also sold to the public. The military ceremony takes place for around 50 minutes in the broad, gravel-covered courtyard of the Rashtrapati Bhavan.

At a briefing by India’s Ministry of External Affairs on Friday, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked about the possibility of the Bangladeshi prime minister visiting India. He said that if there was any such information, it would be shared.

Clearly, the possibility that had emerged of a bilateral visit this month does not appear to be materialising for the time being. However, according to informed circles in both countries, discussions at the government level are continuing on the matter.

No direction on preparations for the visit

Prothom Alo’s diplomatic correspondent reports that when Dhaka’s diplomatic sources were asked about reports published in the Indian media regarding the prime minister’s visit to India next week, they said the reports were not accurate.

Sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs told Prothom Alo that there were no instructions regarding preparations for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s possible visit to Delhi. As a result, there was no opportunity to make preparations for the India visit.

However, multiple government sources told this correspondent in the evening that discussions over the prime minister’s possible visit were continuing under directions from the political leadership of both countries.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister’s Press Secretary Saleh Shibli told Reuters that no decision had yet been made regarding the prime minister’s visit. He said Dhaka was waiting for India’s response on the extradition of Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals.

Midfielder Leandro Paredes and several Argentina team-mates have received bans and fines for their part in clashes with Spain players at the World Cup final, FIFA said on Friday.
In the strongest punishment handed down by world football's governing body, Paredes was banned for 10 international games and fined $90,000.
He grabbed Eric Garcia by the throat and wrestled Spain's Gavi to the ground while holding his substitute's bib, which led to an escalation in the incidents on the field after the final that Spain won 1-0 at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on July 19.
Paredes' teammate Nahuel Molina received a seven-match ban and must also pay a fine of $90,000, while Thiago Almada was suspended for one match and fined $30,000.
Roberto Ayala, a member of Argentina's coaching team, was given a three-match suspension and a fine of $30,000.
Gavi was banned for a match and also fined $30,000 for his role in the fracas that erupted after holders Argentina were defeated thanks to Ferran Torres' goal in extra time.
Argentina have also been ordered to play their next two home matches with capacity reduced to 50 percent, though one match of that sanction is suspended.
Additionally, the Argentinian Football Association (AFA) has been fined $321,000 for breaches of FIFA's disciplinary code relating to using a sports event for making demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.
After Lionel Messi's Argentina beat England 2-1 in a tense World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner saying: "The Falklands are Argentine".
Argentine forces invaded the British overseas territory in the southwest Atlantic Ocean in 1982, which resulted in then-British prime minister Margaret Thatcher sending a naval task force to reclaim them.
The resulting conflict, which lasted for 74 days from April to June 1982, led to the deaths of 655 Argentine and 255 British servicemen. Three people from the islands also died.
The AFA said it would appeal the suspensions and fines.
The AFA said in a statement it would "request from FIFA the grounds for the rulings that are subject to review in order to file appeals before the Appeals Committee".
FIFA had appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to examine the incidents after the final whistle.

item.title: Australia lose three wickets after skittling Bangladesh for 64
item.description:
Australia lost three quick wickets as Bangladesh fought back on day one of the second Test with the hosts 50-3 at tea after a Mitchell Starc masterclass skittled the visitors for just 64.
Skipper Pat Cummins won the toss in Mackay and his bowlers feasted on a fine day, determined to bounce back from a shock nine-wicket loss in the first Test at Darwin.
An irrepressible Starc was the destroyer in an incredible spell of swing and seam, taking five wickets in 22 balls during the morning session.
Bangladesh reached lunch at 35-6 and lasted barely an hour after the break as Starc and Cummins mopped up.
Only a last-wicket partnership of 25 between Taijul Islam (11 not out) and Shoriful Islam (14) took them past their lowest Test score of 43, against the West Indies in 2018.
Starc ended with 6-12 and Cummins took 3-25.
Australia started well in reply but then lost three wickets for 19 runs, leaving Steve Smith (six) and Cameron Green (one) with their work cut out.
Matt Renshaw, recalled for the first time since 2023 when opener Jake Weatherald was axed after Darwin, failed to repay selectors' faith, gone for eight after edging Taskin Ahmed to Tanzid Hasan at third slip.
Fellow opener Travis Head (22) was bowled by Shoriful who missed the first Test with an injury, before he repeated the feat with under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne (4), who was desperate for a big score.
Australia made a stunning start when Starc removed Shadman Islam with the first ball of the day, tempting a leading edge that Green did well to hold in the gully.
It was the fourth time the veteran left-armer has got a wicket with the maiden ball of a Test -- becoming the first player to do so -- and the ninth time he has achieved the feat in the opening over.
The 36-year-old sent Bangladesh's other opener Tanzid packing with the first ball of his second over, caught at slip by Beau Webster, then trapped captain Najmul Hossain Shanto lbw with his next delivery.
It left Bangladesh reeling at 3-9 in the third over.
The experienced Mushfiqur Rahim fended off Starc's hat-trick ball, but he was unstoppable and grabbed his fourth wicket in his third over.
This time, Mominul Haque was the victim in a similar dismissal to Shadman, undone by late swing to send a thick edge low to Green in the gully on nine.
Webster dropped a sitter at slip off Starc in his fourth over, but Litton Das' luck ran out next ball, out lbw on review as the visitors slumped to 5-12.
It was the 19th time Starc has taken five wickets in an innings and achieved in just 22 balls -- the sixth fastest of all-time.
Starc holds the record after taking five in only 15 balls against the West Indies in 2025.
Mushfiqur hung around for 41 balls but he had no answer when Cummins came on, bowled for five.
Cummins struck again after lunch to dismiss Mehidy Hasan Miraz for 11, taken brilliantly by Webster in the slips, before Hazlewood took care of Hasan Mahmud (10) eight balls later.
Bangladesh moved past their lowest Test score as the tailenders hit out, before Starc fittingly wrapped it up with the wicket of Shoriful.
